notes.meaning: About two months after Jerusalem was burned, Ishmael came to Gedaliah, the governor, at Mizpah. Ishmael was from the royal family of David. The commentators think he was jealous that someone else had been put in charge. Gedaliah welcomed him to his table. In those days, eating together was like making a promise of friendship, so the murder that followed was a deep betrayal (compare Psalm 41:9).

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars doubt the short timeline. They think about five years, not two months, may have passed between the fall of the city and the murder.

notes.meaning: While they were at the meal, Ishmael and his ten men rose up and killed Gedaliah with the sword. The verse stresses that Gedaliah had been appointed by the king of Babylon. Killing him showed contempt for Babylon's rule and was sure to bring Babylon's anger on the poor people left in the land. The king of the Ammonites was behind the plot, and later Jews kept a fast day every year to remember this murder.

Ishmael also killed the Jews who were with Gedaliah in the house, and the Babylonian soldiers who served as his guard. They were caught off guard and unarmed. Most of the other people at Mizpah, possibly including Jeremiah, were not killed but taken captive later (v. 10).

The next day, before news of the murder had spread beyond Mizpah, eighty men came from the northern towns of Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria. They were faithful worshippers of the Lord. They had shaved beards, torn clothes and cuts on their bodies, all signs of deep grief over the ruined temple. They brought grain offerings and incense, not animals, to offer at the place where the temple had stood, which was still counted holy. Some commentators note that cutting the body was a pagan custom God's law forbade, while Calvin thought their grief here was sincere and not wrong.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars guessed that Gedaliah had set up a temporary place of worship at Mizpah, since the temple was gone.

notes.meaning: Ishmael went out to meet them, weeping as if he shared their sorrow. His tears were fake, meant to win their trust. He invited them to come and see Gedaliah, hiding the fact that Gedaliah was already dead. The commentators note that wicked people often put on a show of goodness to do harm more easily.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The old Greek translation of the Old Testament says the pilgrims were the ones weeping, not Ishmael. Some scholars think that reading is more natural.

notes.meaning: Once the men were inside the city, Ishmael and his men killed them and threw their bodies into a cistern, a large pit for storing water. The pilgrims were unarmed and could not defend themselves. The reason for this cruelty is not clear. Calvin thought Ishmael suspected they had come to live under Gedaliah, while Keil & Delitzsch saw it as hatred of anything that might help Judah recover.

Ten of the men saved their lives by offering Ishmael their hidden stores of wheat, barley, oil and honey. Farmers in troubled times kept food in secret underground pits. Ishmael's greed was stronger than his cruelty. Matthew Henry adds that riches may sometimes buy a man's life for a while, but no one can bribe death in the end.

The cistern had been made long before by King Asa, when he strengthened Mizpah against Baasha, king of Israel (1 Kings 15:22). It was probably meant to hold water during a siege. Something built to protect God's people now became a grave for His faithful worshippers. Ishmael filled it with the dead.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The words "because of Gedaliah" are hard to read in the original. Some scholars prefer the old Greek reading, which simply says it was a great pit.

notes.meaning: Ishmael then took everyone left at Mizpah as captives, including the king's daughters, meaning princesses of the royal family. He headed for the land of the Ammonites, probably to hand them over or sell them as slaves. Matthew Henry warns that we should never feel too secure in this world. When we think the worst is over, more trouble may come.

Johanan, who had earlier warned Gedaliah about Ishmael, heard what had happened. He gathered his men and chased Ishmael. He caught up with him by the great pool at Gibeon, the same pool mentioned in 2 Samuel 2:13. Matthew Henry notes it would have been better if Johanan had stayed near Gedaliah to guard him in the first place.

When the captives saw Johanan and his army, they were glad. They had only gone with Ishmael because they were forced to. They turned around and went over to Johanan. They were tired of Ishmael's cruelty and seized the first chance to escape.

Ishmael escaped with eight men, so two of his ten were lost, and he fled to the Ammonites. Matthew Henry notes that the most cruel are often the most cowardly. Calvin asks why God let such a murderer go. He answers that God punishes the wicked in many ways and times. Seeing evil go unpunished now should point us to God's final judgment.

Johanan and the other army leaders took charge of all the people they had rescued at Gibeon. These were the remnant, the few left in the land. They included soldiers, women, children and court officials (eunuchs, servants of the royal household). Matthew Henry notes that Johanan gained command honestly, but he would not lead the people any better than Ishmael had.

They stopped at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, a resting place linked to Chimham, son of Barzillai, whom David had rewarded (2 Samuel 19:37-38). They planned to go on to Egypt because they feared the Babylonians would take revenge for Gedaliah's murder. Calvin says the fear had some reason, but they could have cleared themselves by blaming the real killer. Going to Egypt went against God's word, and Matthew Henry warns against using fears as an excuse to sin.
